title: The Language of DNA
description: What DNA is, how it's structured, and how it encodes life

concepts.title: DNA Structure
concepts.contentHtml:
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is the molecule that stores hereditary information in all known life. It's a double helix — two strands wound around each other, connected by base pairs.

There are four bases: Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C). A always pairs with T; G always pairs with C. This complementary pairing, discovered by Watson and Crick in 1953 using Rosalind Franklin's X-ray data, is the key to copying DNA.

A human cell packs about 6 billion base pairs (two copies of the 3-billion-base-pair genome) into 46 chromosomes, roughly 2 metres of DNA coiled tightly in a nucleus just 6 micrometres wide.

concepts.title: Genes and the Genetic Code
concepts.contentHtml:
A gene is a stretch of DNA that encodes instructions for making a protein. The human genome contains roughly 20,000–25,000 protein-coding genes.

The genetic code translates nucleotide sequences into amino acids using codons — triplets of three bases. For example, AUG codes for methionine and acts as the start codon. There are 64 codons encoding 20 amino acids, so the code is redundant (multiple codons can specify the same amino acid).

Crucially, only about 1.5% of human DNA codes for proteins. Much of the rest regulates genes, has structural roles, or is still poorly understood.

concepts.title: DNA Replication
concepts.contentHtml:
Before a cell divides, it must copy its DNA precisely. DNA replication is semi-conservative: each old strand serves as a template for a new complementary strand, producing two identical double helices.

The enzyme DNA polymerase reads the template and adds matching bases at extraordinary speed — about 1,000 bases per second in bacteria, with an error rate of roughly 1 in a billion after proofreading and mismatch repair.

This fidelity matters enormously: an error in a critical gene can cause disease or cancer. Helicase unwinds the helix; primase lays a starter RNA primer; DNA polymerase then extends the new strand.

title: From Gene to Protein
description: Transcription, translation, and how DNA becomes working molecules

concepts.title: Transcription
concepts.contentHtml:
Transcription is the first step of gene expression: a gene's DNA sequence is copied into a complementary strand of mRNA (messenger RNA) by the enzyme RNA polymerase.

RNA is similar to DNA but uses Uracil (U) instead of Thymine, and is single-stranded. The mRNA transcript carries the gene's message out of the nucleus to the cytoplasm.

In eukaryotes, the initial transcript is processed: introns (non-coding sections) are spliced out and exons are joined. A 5' cap and poly-A tail are added for stability. The mature mRNA is then ready for translation.

concepts.title: Translation
concepts.contentHtml:
Translation converts the mRNA sequence into a protein at the ribosome. Transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules act as adaptors: each carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon that matches a codon on the mRNA.

The ribosome moves along the mRNA in triplets. Each matching tRNA delivers its amino acid, which is added to the growing protein chain. When a stop codon (UAA, UAG, or UGA) is reached, the chain is released.

A single mRNA can be read by multiple ribosomes simultaneously (a polysome), producing many protein copies at once. This entire flow — DNA → mRNA → protein — is called the central dogma of molecular biology.

concepts.title: Mutations and Their Effects
concepts.contentHtml:
A mutation is a heritable change in the DNA sequence. Point mutations change a single base: a missense mutation changes one amino acid; a nonsense mutation creates a premature stop codon; a silent mutation changes the codon but not the amino acid (due to redundancy).

Frameshift mutations (insertions or deletions) shift the reading frame, scrambling all downstream codons. Sickle-cell anaemia is caused by a single missense mutation in haemoglobin: GAG → GTG, changing glutamate to valine and distorting the protein's shape.

Not all mutations are harmful — some are neutral; a rare few are beneficial and become the raw material for evolution.

title: Inheritance Patterns
description: Mendel's laws, dominance, and why traits are inherited the way they are

concepts.title: Mendelian Inheritance
concepts.contentHtml:
Gregor Mendel, working with pea plants in the 1860s, deduced two fundamental laws of heredity. His Law of Segregation states that each organism has two alleles for each trait, and these separate during gamete formation so each gamete carries one allele.

His Law of Independent Assortment states that genes on different chromosomes segregate independently.

An organism with two identical alleles (AA or aa) is homozygous; two different alleles (Aa) is heterozygous. A Punnett square predicts offspring ratios. Cross Aa × Aa: 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa genotype; 3 dominant : 1 recessive phenotype.

concepts.title: Dominance and Incomplete Dominance
concepts.contentHtml:
In complete dominance, one allele fully masks the other. A single copy of the dominant allele (A_) produces the dominant phenotype. But dominance is not universal.

In incomplete dominance, heterozygotes have an intermediate phenotype — red × white snapdragons produce pink offspring. In codominance, both alleles are fully expressed — human AB blood type expresses both A and B antigens simultaneously.

The ABO blood group system also illustrates multiple alleles: there are three alleles (I^A, I^B, i) but any one person carries only two of them.

concepts.title: Sex Linkage and Pedigrees
concepts.contentHtml:
Sex chromosomes determine biological sex in humans: XX for females, XY for males. The X chromosome carries many genes the Y lacks. Traits encoded on the X chromosome are X-linked.

Red-green colour blindness and haemophilia are X-linked recessive. Females need two copies of the recessive allele to express it; males need only one (they have no second X). This is why these conditions are far more common in males.

Pedigree charts track traits across generations: squares are males, circles females, filled symbols are affected individuals. Reading pedigrees can reveal whether a trait is dominant, recessive, or X-linked.

title: Gene Regulation
description: How cells control which genes are switched on or off

concepts.title: The Lac Operon
concepts.contentHtml:
Every cell in your body has the same DNA, yet a liver cell and a neuron look and behave very differently. Gene regulation is the mechanism of selectively switching genes on or off.

The classic model is the lac operon in E. coli, discovered by Jacob and Monod. When lactose is absent, a repressor protein blocks the operator, silencing the genes needed to digest lactose. When lactose is present, it binds the repressor, releasing it — and the genes are expressed.

This elegant on/off switch shows that genes are responsive to the environment, not always running at full blast.

concepts.title: Epigenetics
concepts.contentHtml:
Epigenetics refers to heritable changes in gene expression that do not alter the DNA sequence itself. Two main mechanisms: DNA methylation (adding a methyl group to cytosine, typically silencing genes) and histone modification (histones are proteins DNA wraps around; modifications compact or loosen the DNA, affecting accessibility).

Epigenetic marks can be influenced by environment — diet, stress, toxins — and some can be passed to offspring. The Dutch Hunger Winter (1944–45) showed that famine experienced in the womb left epigenetic marks affecting metabolism decades later.

Epigenetics helps explain how identical twins can diverge in health outcomes over time despite identical DNA sequences.

concepts.title: RNA Interference
concepts.contentHtml:
Cells also regulate genes post-transcriptionally. RNA interference (RNAi) uses small RNA molecules to silence specific mRNAs before they can be translated.

MicroRNAs (miRNA) are endogenous ~22-nucleotide RNAs that bind complementary sequences on mRNAs, blocking translation or triggering degradation. Over 2,000 human miRNAs regulate perhaps 60% of all protein-coding genes.

RNAi was discovered by Andrew Fire and Craig Mello, who won the 2006 Nobel Prize. It has become a powerful research tool and is being developed as therapeutics — inclisiran, an FDA-approved siRNA drug, silences a cholesterol gene in the liver to treat high LDL.

title: CRISPR and the Genome Editing Revolution
description: How we now rewrite DNA — and what that means for medicine and ethics

concepts.title: How CRISPR-Cas9 Works
concepts.contentHtml:
CRISPR-Cas9 is a genome-editing tool adapted from a bacterial immune system. Bacteria store snippets of viral DNA in their genome as a molecular memory. When the same virus attacks again, they produce RNA that guides the Cas9 protein to the viral DNA, which Cas9 then cuts.

Scientists, principally Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier (2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry), adapted this into a universal tool: design a guide RNA complementary to any target sequence, deliver it with Cas9, and Cas9 cuts that exact spot in any cell's genome.

This is far cheaper and more precise than older tools (zinc-finger nucleases, TALENs). A single researcher can now edit a gene in weeks rather than years.

concepts.title: Medical Applications
concepts.contentHtml:
CRISPR is already yielding treatments. In 2023, Casgevy became the first approved CRISPR-based therapy — it cures sickle-cell disease and beta-thalassaemia by reactivating the foetal haemoglobin gene, bypassing the defective adult haemoglobin gene.

Other clinical trials target cancers (editing immune T cells to recognise tumours), HIV (excising viral DNA from infected cells), and inherited blindness (editing photoreceptor genes in the eye).

Gene editing is also being used in pigs to knock out rejection-causing genes, making pig organs (xenotransplantation) potentially viable for human transplant. In 2024, a man survived months with a gene-edited pig kidney.

concepts.title: Ethics and Germline Editing
concepts.contentHtml:
CRISPR edits can be somatic (in body cells, not heritable) or germline (in embryos/sperm/eggs, passed to all descendants). Somatic edits are broadly accepted; germline editing is deeply controversial.

In 2018, He Jiankui shocked the scientific community by creating the first gene-edited babies — twin girls with CCR5 mutations intended to confer HIV resistance. He was widely condemned, imprisoned in China, and the experiment raised major safety concerns (off-target edits, unknown long-term effects).

Key debates: who decides which traits are 'diseases' versus enhancements? Could germline editing create heritable disparities? Clinical germline editing is prohibited in many countries, and leading scientists have called for a global moratorium.

concepts.title: What Is Epigenetics?
concepts.contentHtml:
Epigenetics studies heritable changes in gene expression that don't change DNA sequence. Two main mechanisms: DNA methylation and histone modifications.

DNA methylation: methyl groups on cytosine nucleotides (especially in CpG dinucleotides) typically silence genes. Methylation patterns are inherited across cell divisions but can be reprogrammed.

Histone modifications: acetylation (H3K9ac, H3K27ac) generally activates genes; methylation can either activate or repress depending on the residue and number of methyls.

concepts.title: Epigenetic Regulation in Development & Disease
concepts.contentHtml:
Cell types differ in their epigenome more than their genome. The same DNA in liver, neuron, and skin cells is differently methylated and histone-marked, producing different transcription programs.

X-inactivation: in female mammalian cells, one X chromosome is randomly silenced via Xist RNA and heterochromatin marks. This produces calico cat coat patterns (different X-linked color genes silenced in patches of cells).

Disease epigenetics: cancer cells have widely abnormal methylation; psychiatric conditions show epigenomic correlates; epigenetic inheritance of trauma is debated but real for some traits in plants and animals.

concepts.title: Therapeutic Epigenetics
concepts.contentHtml:
Several drugs target epigenetic enzymes:

• 5-azacytidine (DNA methyltransferase inhibitor) treats myelodysplastic syndrome.
• HDAC inhibitors (vorinostat, romidepsin) treat cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.
• EZH2 inhibitors (tazemetostat) treat follicular lymphoma.

Epigenetic drugs reactivate silenced tumor suppressors or modify gene expression broadly. The field is expanding rapidly.

concepts.title: Allele Frequencies & Hardy-Weinberg
concepts.contentHtml:
Population genetics tracks allele frequencies — the proportion of a gene's variants in a population — over generations.

The Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium describes the null state: in an infinitely large randomly mating population without selection or mutation, allele frequencies stay constant. p² + 2pq + q² = 1.

Real populations deviate. Each deviation tells us something — selection acting, drift in small populations, structure (subpopulations), assortative mating, or new mutations.

concepts.title: Selection, Drift, Migration
concepts.contentHtml:
Four forces change allele frequencies: selection (different fitness of genotypes), drift (random sampling effects, especially in small populations), migration (gene flow between populations), and mutation (new alleles introduced).

Genetic drift is strongest in small populations — explains why isolated island populations or those passing through bottlenecks (founder events) lose diversity.

Modern population genomics uses entire genome sequences from many individuals to estimate these forces precisely. Reveals migrations, ancient admixture, selection on specific genes.

concepts.title: Human Genetic Variation
concepts.contentHtml:
Two random humans typically differ at ~3 million sites in their 3-billion-base genomes — about 0.1%. We're remarkably similar. Most variation is shared across populations; ancestry signals are subtle.

SNPs (single nucleotide polymorphisms) underlie much variation. Some are functional (altering proteins or expression); most are silent or in non-coding DNA.

GWAS (genome-wide association studies) link SNPs to traits or diseases. They've identified thousands of loci affecting height, BMI, cardiovascular disease, schizophrenia. Most effects are tiny; complex traits are highly polygenic.

title: Genomics & Personalized Medicine
description: From sequencing the genome to using it

concepts.title: The Human Genome
concepts.contentHtml:
The Human Genome Project (1990-2003) produced the first reference human genome. Cost: ~$3 billion. Modern individual genome sequencing: ~$200 and falling, in hours.

The human genome has ~20,000 protein-coding genes — fewer than expected. Most of the genome is non-coding (regulatory, structural, junk). The 'ENCODE' project mapped ~80% of the genome as 'biochemically active.'

concepts.title: Pharmacogenomics
concepts.contentHtml:
Genetic variants in drug-metabolizing enzymes (CYPs especially) and drug targets explain why people respond differently to the same dose.

Examples: warfarin dosing (CYP2C9, VKORC1 variants); clopidogrel response (CYP2C19); cancer drug response based on tumor mutations (HER2 status, EGFR mutations, BRCA mutations).

Many regulatory bodies now mandate or recommend genetic testing before certain prescriptions. Pre-emptive pharmacogenomic profiling is being implemented in some healthcare systems.

concepts.title: Privacy and Ethics
concepts.contentHtml:
Direct-to-consumer genetics (23andMe, AncestryDNA) has put millions of personal genomes into databases. Privacy concerns are significant: genomes reveal health risks, ancestry, family relationships including unknown ones.

The Golden State Killer case (2018) used a genealogy database to identify a suspect from distant relatives' DNA. Familial DNA matching has solved many cold cases — and raised questions about consent.

Genetic discrimination, insurance access, gene patents, and the right to genetic privacy are active legal and ethical debates. The technology has outrun regulation.
